units.translation: Of this word, about which see Thes. vol. 5 p. 2302, only three cases are in use: the dual ὄσσε [the two eyes], the plural ὄσσων [of the eyes] and ὄσσοις [to/with the eyes].
Thus I emended what is in M τόσσων περ εὔφρων [so many kindly] and added the words Διός κόρα [daughters of Zeus]: about which I spoke in the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. LXXXIV.

The contracted form ὀστοῦν [bone] the grammarians assign to Attic, the uncontracted ὀστέον [bone], which epic and tragic poets mostly use, to the common dialect. On both see Thes. vol. 5 p. 2305.

which is usually written separately as ὅ τι [whatever] or with a diastole as ὅ, τι [whatever], to distinguish it from the conjunction ὅτι [that]
The meaning of this pronoun is the same as that of the simple ὅς [who], except that ὅς is definite, while ὅστις is indefinite: someone who, everyone who, whoever, such as.
ὅστις [whoever] in clauses added for the purpose of explaining or giving a reason.
ὅστις [whoever], preceded by the interrogative pronoun ἐστὶν τίς [who is it?].
In indirect question
ὅστις [whoever] with the subjunctive.
ὅστις [whoever] with the optative.
